html:
British North America was the set of English, later British, colonies on the Atlantic coast of North America, from the founding of Jamestown in Virginia in 1607 until thirteen of them declared independence in 1776.

The colonies grew in very different ways:

  • Virginia and the South lived on tobacco, then rice and indigo, grown first by indentured servants and then, more and more, by enslaved Africans (see Virginia tobacco boom and enslaved Africans reach Virginia).
  • New England was settled by Puritans seeking a godly society (see Puritan migration and the Mayflower Compact). It lived by farming, fishing, timber and trade.
  • The middle colonies included New York, taken from the Dutch in 1664, and Pennsylvania, founded by Quakers. They were the most mixed in religion and origin.

Each colony had its own elected assembly, which gave colonists long practice in governing themselves. Their growth pushed onto the lands of Native peoples, who were also hit hard by disease and war. To the north lay New France, and the two empires fought a long series of wars, often with Native allies such as the Haudenosaunee.

Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War in 1763 removed France from Canada but left large debts. New taxes from London, imposed without colonial votes, led to protest and then to the American Revolutionary War. The Declaration of Independence of 1776 created the United States. The northern colonies, Canada and Nova Scotia, stayed British and grew into Canada.
sum: British North America was the set of English, later British, colonies on the Atlantic coast of North America, from the founding of Jamestown in Virginia in 1607 until thirteen of them declared independence in 1776.
